_about: Snapshot of octopus-mma technique text and pose JSON. Generated by scripts/snapshot-mma.mjs; do not hand-edit. A fix in mma reaches health only by re-running the script.

moves.title: Bob and Weave
moves.summary: Ducking under a hook by bending the knees and moving the head in a U-shape — used to avoid wide punches and emerge in position to counter.
steps: As a hook approaches, bend your knees to drop your head below the level of the incoming punch — do not just hinge at the waist.
Move your upper body in a U-shape: down and to the outside of the punch, then back up on the other side.
The entire movement is driven by the legs; the back stays relatively straight.
As you come up on the other side, your weight loads naturally for a hook or uppercut counter.
Return to a balanced stance immediately after the counter.
keyPoints: Bend the knees first — a bob that uses the waist rather than the legs is slow and breaks your structure.
The U-shape should be compact; a wide, exaggerated dip is slow and leaves you off-balance.
Coming up on the outside of a hook puts you in a dominant position for a right-hand counter.
Keep both hands at cheek level throughout — your guard does not drop during the bob.
Combine with a lead hook or right uppercut for maximum effectiveness.

moves.title: Cross
moves.summary: The rear-hand straight punch — the hardest power shot in a boxer's arsenal, driven by full hip and shoulder rotation.
steps: From your orthodox stance, initiate the cross by pushing off the rear foot and pivoting on the ball of that foot.
Rotate your hips and torso toward the target — the power comes from this rotation, not the arm alone.
Extend the rear hand straight toward the target, rotating the fist palm-down at full extension while the shoulder drives forward.
Keep the lead hand tight to your cheek to protect from a counter jab.
Snap the rear hand back as the hip rotation reverses, returning immediately to your guard.
keyPoints: The pivot of the rear foot is where the power originates — no pivot, no power.
The shoulder should brush past your chin as the punch extends, protecting it from counters.
Drive through the target, not just to it, for maximum penetration.
The cross works best after a jab has occupied your opponent's attention (jab-cross is the fundamental combination).
Body crosses to the liver are just as effective as head crosses — vary your levels.

moves.title: Hook
moves.summary: A short arc punch thrown at 90° that travels around the opponent's guard — one of the most powerful and frequently landed punches in boxing.
steps: From your orthodox stance, transfer your weight slightly onto the lead foot.
Rotate your lead hip and shoulder toward the target simultaneously, pivoting on the ball of the lead foot.
Keep the lead forearm parallel to the ground, elbow bent at roughly 90°, and swing the fist in a tight horizontal arc — do not loop it wide.
The fist travels along the arc until impact; the knuckles land on the side of the jaw or temple.
Immediately rotate back and return the hand to your cheek, keeping the rear hand up throughout.
keyPoints: Elbow height matters: a hook thrown with the elbow too low becomes a slap; too high and it loses power.
The power comes from hip and shoulder rotation — a hook with no body rotation is weak.
Keep the arc tight; a wide looping hook is slow, telegraphed, and easy to see coming.
The lead hook to the body (liver shot) is executed the same way but aimed downward at the floating rib.
In combinations, the hook naturally follows the cross because the weight is already shifting to the lead side.

moves.title: Jab
moves.summary: The lead-hand straight punch — boxing's most important weapon for range-finding, disruption, and setting up combinations.
steps: Start in your orthodox stance with both hands at your cheeks.
Extend the lead hand straight out toward the target, rotating the fist palm-down at full extension.
As the jab extends, push off the rear foot slightly and roll the lead shoulder forward to add reach.
Snap the hand back to your cheek immediately after impact — do not let it hang out.
Return to your guard and reset your stance.
keyPoints: Speed matters more than power; a fast jab is more useful than a slow hard one.
Keep the rear hand glued to your cheek throughout — you are vulnerable to a counter cross during the jab.
Roll the shoulder forward to protect the chin and add a few inches of reach.
The jab can target the head or be dipped to the body to change levels.
Throw it constantly — even a light jab disrupts an opponent's rhythm.

moves.title: Orthodox Stance
moves.summary: The foundational fighting position for right-handed boxers — weight balanced, guard up, and body angled to minimise the target.
steps: Stand with your feet shoulder-width apart, then step your left foot forward so your feet are staggered roughly one shoulder-width in depth.
Angle your body about 45° to your opponent so your left side faces them — this narrows your target profile.
Bend both knees slightly and distribute your weight evenly across both feet; stay on the balls of your feet.
Raise both hands: left fist in front of your left cheek (lead hand), right fist beside your right cheek (rear hand). Elbows tucked down to protect the ribs.
Keep your chin slightly tucked and look over the knuckles of your lead hand.
keyPoints: The rear heel lifts slightly off the ground, keeping you light on your feet.
Shoulders are relaxed — tension kills speed.
The lead shoulder angles forward, providing passive defence for the chin.
Keep elbows close to the body; flared elbows expose the liver and ribs.
This stance applies to right-handed (orthodox) fighters. Left-handed fighters mirror it (southpaw).

moves.title: Slip
moves.summary: Moving the head offline by rotating the upper body to let a straight punch pass beside the face — the cornerstone of elusive boxing defence.
steps: As a straight punch approaches, rotate your upper body slightly to the outside of the punch — slip to the outside of a jab by rotating right; slip to the outside of a cross by rotating left.
Bend slightly at the waist as you rotate, lowering the head a few inches so the punch passes beside and above.
Keep both hands up throughout — the slip is a body movement, not a hand movement.
Your weight shifts slightly onto the lead foot when slipping to the right, onto the rear foot when slipping left.
Return to centre immediately and counter with the appropriate punch (e.g., a right cross after slipping the jab to the outside).
keyPoints: The movement is small — a few inches is all you need. Big lurching slips kill your balance and take you out of counter range.
Keep the chin tucked throughout; slipping with the chin up is an invitation for an uppercut.
Slipping to the outside of a jab puts you in the safest position and sets up a right-hand counter.
Slipping to the inside of a cross is riskier but sets up a left hook counter.
Practise slipping on a double-end bag or with a partner to develop timing.

moves.title: Uppercut
moves.summary: An upward-rising punch that drives vertically under an opponent's guard — devastating at close range and in combination.
steps: From your orthodox stance, dip slightly by bending the lead-side knee — this loads the punch without telegraphing a big wind-up.
Drive upward from the legs and rotate the lead hip forward and upward, as though scooping.
The lead arm rises in a tight vertical arc, palm facing you at impact, making contact with the first two knuckles under the chin.
Do not let the punch travel past face height — stop and snap back immediately.
Return to your guard; the rear hand stays at your cheek throughout.
keyPoints: The power comes from the leg drive and hip rise, not from swinging the arm up.
Keep the punch close to the body — a wide arm swing telegraphs and weakens the punch.
The rear uppercut follows the same mechanics using the rear side and is generally the harder punch.
At body range, aim the uppercut at the solar plexus or liver rather than the chin.
The uppercut is most effective when your opponent's head is positioned forward, or after a slip to the outside.

moves.title: Rising Block
moves.summary: Age Uke drives the forearm upward and forward to deflect descending strikes away from the head — equivalent to the Taekwondo high block but with a more compact wind-up.
steps: Begin in Zenkutsu-dachi (front stance) or moving stance.
Wind up: bring the blocking arm across the body, fist near the opposite hip, palm facing outward.
Drive the blocking arm upward in an arc — the forearm rises and crosses in front of the face as it ascends.
Finish with the forearm above the forehead, angled forward at roughly 45°. The fist is at forehead height or slightly above. Palm faces outward.
Pull the reaction hand (Hikite) sharply back to the hip, palm-up, as the block completes.
Kime at the endpoint.
keyPoints: The finishing position angles the forearm forward at 45° — not horizontal (no deflection angle) and not vertical (blocks vision).
The blocking surface is the outer forearm (little-finger side).
In Shotokan, the wind-up starts from the opposite hip rather than the ear-level position common in some other styles. The arc is compact but fast.
The elbow of the blocking arm should not lock out fully — it remains bent, maintaining structural strength.
Eyes must remain visible over the forearm — the block is above the forehead, not in front of the face.

moves.title: Downward Block
moves.summary: Gedan Barai sweeps the forearm downward across the body to deflect low attacks — the first block taught in karate and the opening move of Heian Shodan.
steps: Begin in Zenkutsu-dachi (front stance) or Yoi (ready position).
Wind up: raise the blocking arm to the opposite shoulder, crossing in front of the body. The fist is near the opposite ear, elbow pointing outward, palm facing inward toward the head.
Simultaneously raise the other arm as the reaction arm — it will pull back to the hip.
Drive the blocking arm downward in a sweeping arc: the forearm sweeps across the body and finishes low — fist approximately 10cm above the front thigh, on the outside of the lead leg.
Pull the reaction hand sharply back to the hip, palm-up (Hikite).
Kime (focus): tighten the arm, fist, and core sharply at the endpoint.
keyPoints: The finishing position is low — the fist is near the thigh, not at the hip or navel. The forearm angles downward across the front thigh.
The blocking surface is the outer forearm (the same side as the little finger).
The wind-up (raising the arm to the opposite shoulder) creates the arc that generates sweeping power.
Hikite (the reaction hand pulling back to the hip) is as important as the block itself — it creates the counter-rotation that doubles the speed.
In Shotokan kata, Gedan Barai is executed with kiai and maximum kime at the endpoint.

moves.title: Reverse Punch
moves.summary: Gyaku Zuki is the reverse punch — the rear hand strikes across the body from front stance, using hip rotation as the primary power source.
steps: Begin in left Zenkutsu Dachi (left foot forward): left fist extended (from Oi Zuki or a block), right fist chambered at the right hip, palm-up.
Initiate a powerful hip rotation — drive the right hip sharply forward and the left hip back. This is the engine of the technique.
As the hip rotates, drive the right fist forward in a straight line toward the target. At Chudan level (solar plexus); at Jodan level (face) for face punch variation.
The fist rotates 180° during the extension — palm-up at the hip, palm-down at full extension. The rotation occurs at the very end.
Pull the left fist back sharply to the left hip simultaneously (Hikite).
Kime at full extension: the hips, core, shoulder, arm, and fist all lock together for an instant.
keyPoints: The hip is the origin of power, not the shoulder and not the arm. If you can feel your hip rotating when you punch, you are doing it correctly.
The fist travels in a perfectly straight line — no arc, no rising curve. The elbow tracks close to the ribs throughout.
Kime must involve the entire body: the stance, the core, the shoulder, and the arm lock together at the moment of impact. A soft kime wastes all the power generated by the hip rotation.
The rotation of the fist (palm-down at extension) adds a small torque component but, more importantly, it is a signal that the arm is fully extended and kime is occurring.
Hikite is not optional — its opposing pull generates the counter-rotation that makes the striking-side rotation faster.

moves.title: Lunge Punch
moves.summary: Oi Zuki is the lunge punch — a full stepping punch where the same-side hand as the stepping foot delivers the strike, channelling the momentum of the step into the punch.
steps: Begin in Zenkutsu-dachi (left leg forward), right fist extended from a previous technique, left fist chambered at the left hip.
Step forward with the right foot, moving into right Zenkutsu-dachi.
As the right foot travels forward, chamber the right fist back to the right hip, palm-up.
As the right foot lands, drive the right fist forward in a straight line to the target (Chudan — solar plexus level, or Jodan — face level).
The fist rotates from palm-up to palm-down during the punch — the rotation completes at the moment of impact.
Pull the left fist sharply back to the left hip simultaneously (Hikite).
Kime as the foot lands and the fist reaches full extension — the whole body locks for an instant.
keyPoints: Timing is the essence: the punch and the footfall must be simultaneous — not the punch before, not after.
The travel of the punching fist is a straight line — it does not arc or swing wide.
The elbow tracks close to the ribs during the punch and ends pointing directly backward.
The fist rotation happens at the very end of the extension, producing a snap rather than a rotation-throughout punch.
The body drops slightly as the front foot lands into the deep Zenkutsu-dachi — this drop adds mass to the impact.

moves.title: Front Stance
moves.summary: Zenkutsu Dachi is the primary karate kata stance — a long, low, forward-weighted position that generates power for both blocks and punches.
steps: Stand with feet together, then step forward approximately two shoulder-widths — significantly longer than a normal step.
Bend the front knee deeply — in Shotokan, the front thigh should approach parallel to the floor (knee above the toes, not past them).
Keep the rear leg fully extended and straight — locked at the knee, no bend.
The front foot points directly forward. The rear foot turns outward approximately 45°.
Push the rear heel firmly into the ground — it must not lift.
Distribute weight approximately 60% on the front leg, 40% on the rear.
Keep the hips squared forward and the spine upright — do not lean forward or allow the hips to twist sideways.
keyPoints: The rear leg must be completely straight — any bend in the rear knee raises the stance and reduces its power base.
The front knee tracks directly over the big toe of the front foot — it must not cave inward.
In Shotokan, the stance is deliberately very long and low — beginning students consistently make it too short.
The rear heel stays on the ground throughout. Lifting it collapses the stance.
Hip rotation in this stance drives the power of both Oi Zuki and Gyaku Zuki — a stable Zenkutsu Dachi enables effective hip rotation.

moves.title: Body Kick
moves.summary: The signature Thai roundhouse at rib height: the hips turn all the way over and the shin swings through the body like a bat.
steps: From the stance, step out slightly with the lead foot at an angle and rise onto its ball.
Turn the hips over as the rear leg swings up, the knee nearly straight.
Lean the shoulders back and away to counterbalance the leg, without leaning so far you lose sight of the target.
Swing the rear arm down and back, keeping the lead glove at the face.
Land with the shin across the ribs and kick through, then bring the leg back to the stance.
keyPoints: Height comes from the hip turn and the pivot, not from lifting the knee.
Kick through the target, not at it.
The lean is a counterbalance: the head moves back and away as the leg comes up, and is protected by the lead glove.
Set it up with the jab or the teep; the opponent's hands come up for a punch and the ribs open.
A kick that lands on the arm still scores and still hurts; keep throwing it.

moves.title: Cross
moves.summary: The rear-hand straight punch, powered by the rear leg and hip turn — and the natural set-up for a lead hook or a low kick.
steps: From the stance, lift the rear heel and begin turning it outward.
Drive off the rear foot, rotating the hips and then the shoulders toward the target.
Extend the rear hand straight to the target, turning the fist palm-down at the end.
Keep the lead glove high on the brow, and the chin tucked behind the rear shoulder.
Bring the hand straight back to the guard as the hips turn back.
keyPoints: Rear foot, hip, shoulder, hand — in that order.
The rear heel turns out; if it stays flat, the hips cannot turn.
The lead glove stays on your face: the cross opens you to a lead hook or a lead kick.
Do not overreach. In Muay Thai, leaning onto the lead leg gets it kicked.
Jab–cross–low kick (1–2–kick) is the first combination every beginner learns.

moves.title: Diagonal Knee (Khao Chiang)
moves.summary: The rear knee arcing in at about 45 degrees to the ribs, with the hips turning over: the knee that goes around the guard instead of through it.
steps: From the guard, cock the rear leg back and out to the side; the hips begin to turn away.
Turn the hips over, pivoting on the ball of the lead foot, and swing the knee in at about 45 degrees to the ribs.
Lean the upper body away from the knee to balance, keeping the lead hand high.
Strike with the point of the knee, toes pointed down.
Put the foot back down behind you and return to the guard.
keyPoints: The angle is the point: the knee goes around the elbows, not into them.
The hips turn over, as in a body kick. Without the hip turn it is only a leg swing.
Toes pointed, which tightens the knee joint into a hard point.
Lean away from the knee to balance it, but keep looking at the opponent.
In the clinch, pull the opponent's head to the opposite side, which opens the ribs.

moves.title: Footwork: Step and Pivot
moves.summary: Moving without breaking the stance: step and follow forward and back, and pivot on the lead foot to change angle.
steps: From your stance, push off the rear foot and slide the lead foot forward a half step, keeping it low.
Let the rear foot follow by exactly the same distance, so the stance is restored.
To retreat, push off the lead foot and step the rear foot back a half step first, then let the lead foot follow.
To pivot, keep your weight on the ball of the lead foot and swing the rear foot around in an arc (a quarter turn is plenty), turning the hips and shoulders with it.
After every step or pivot, check that the stance has the same width and the guard has not moved.
keyPoints: The foot nearest the direction of travel moves first; never cross the feet.
Small steps. A half step keeps you balanced and ready to kick or check at any time.
Keep the weight on the rear leg as you step, so the lead leg is still free to check.
The pivot is on the ball of the lead foot, and the whole body turns together.
Moving backward in a straight line is how fighters get trapped; step back and then pivot off the line.

moves.title: Head Kick (Te Kan Kho)
moves.summary: The Thai roundhouse thrown to the neck: step out, rise on the ball of the lead foot and turn the hips all the way over so the shin swings up into the jaw.
steps: From the guard, step the lead foot out at an angle, landing on the ball of the foot.
Rise up on the ball of that foot and start to swing the rear leg; the hips begin to turn.
Turn the hips all the way over and swing the leg up, nearly straight, so the shin lands on the neck and jaw.
Swing the same-side arm down and back for balance; keep the other glove on your own face.
Bring the leg back the way it came and put the foot back under you in the guard.
keyPoints: The hips do the work. The leg follows the hips up; it is not lifted by the thigh.
Rise on the ball of the lead foot and pivot it, heel turning toward the opponent. A flat foot cannot turn far enough.
The leg is close to straight at impact. Strike with the lower shin, not the foot.
Keep a glove on your own face: the head kick leaves you open to a counter.
Set it up: a jab, a cross, or body kicks first so the guard comes down.

moves.title: Hook: Lead and Rear
moves.summary: A short, bent-arm punch that travels around the guard, thrown with the lead or the rear hand and powered by the hip turn.
steps: Lead hook: shift your weight slightly onto the lead foot.
Pivot on the ball of the lead foot and turn the hips and shoulders to the right; the arm comes along with the body, elbow bent and level with the fist.
Land with the knuckles or the palm-down fist, then let the body turn bring the hand back to the guard.
Rear hook: turn the rear heel out, rotate the hips to the left, and bring the rear arm around in the same bent-arm shape.
Keep the non-punching glove on the brow for both.
keyPoints: The hook is thrown with the hips and feet; the arm is a fixed shape that rides the turn.
Elbow at the level of the fist, not below it, for a head hook.
Keep it short. A wide hook is slow and opens you to a straight punch or a teep.
The lead hook is the natural follow-up to the cross (1–2–3).
Lowering the level and hooking to the body sets up the head kick on the same side.

moves.title: Horizontal Elbow (Sok Tat)
moves.summary: The point of the elbow sliced across at eye height, powered by the turn of the hips and shoulders like a short hook.
steps: From the guard, step in to close range.
Raise the elbow to shoulder height with the fist by your ear, forearm roughly parallel to the floor.
Turn the hips and shoulders together and slice the point of the elbow across at eye height.
Follow through, then bring the arm back to cover your face.
Return to the guard.
keyPoints: Strike with the point of the elbow, or just in front of it on the forearm. That is what cuts.
The turn of the hips and shoulders is the power. The arm stays folded and rides the turn.
Keep the other glove on your face; at elbow range the opponent can elbow back.
Close the distance first. An elbow thrown from punching range is a miss.
It comes after a punch or out of the clinch, when the opponent is already close.

moves.title: Jab
moves.summary: The lead-hand straight punch: it measures distance, blinds the opponent and sets up the cross and the kicks.
steps: Start in your Muay Thai stance, gloves at the brow.
Extend the lead hand straight to the target, turning the fist palm-down just before contact.
Let the lead shoulder rise to cover the chin, and take a small step with the lead foot if you need the range.
Keep the rear glove on the brow throughout.
Bring the hand straight back along the same line to the guard, as fast as it went out.
keyPoints: Straight out, straight back: the return is part of the punch.
The rear glove never leaves your face; the counter to a jab is the opponent's cross or kick.
Weight stays mostly back. A Thai jab does not lunge, so you are still ready to check a kick.
Use it to blind and to measure: a jab followed by a rear kick is the classic Muay Thai combination.
It can go to the body too, to bring the opponent's hands down.

moves.title: Low Kick
moves.summary: The Thai roundhouse to the thigh: turn the hips over, swing a nearly straight leg and chop the outside of the opponent's thigh with the shin.
steps: Step the lead foot slightly out to the left at an angle and rise onto its ball, turning the heel toward the target.
Swing the rear leg up and around, the knee only slightly bent, turning the hips over.
Strike the outside of the opponent's thigh with the lower shin, just above the knee to mid-thigh.
Let the rear arm swing down and back for counterbalance and power, while the lead glove stays high to cover the face.
Return the leg along the same path to the stance (or let it swing through and step down if the kick missed).
keyPoints: The shin is the weapon, not the foot. Aim to land the bone a hand's width below the knee.
The pivot on the standing foot is what allows the hips to turn over.
The kick is a swing, not a snap: keep the leg almost straight and kick through the target.
Set it up with punches: jab–cross–low kick, or cross–lead hook–low kick.
The lead glove covers the face: the counter to a low kick is a punch over the top.

moves.title: Muay Thai Stance
moves.summary: The upright, square-ish Thai stance: weight on the rear leg, lead heel light, gloves at the brow — built to check kicks and teep at any moment.
steps: Stand with your feet about shoulder width apart, then step the left foot forward (orthodox) so the lead toes and rear heel are roughly on one line, a little wider than that for balance.
Turn the hips and shoulders only slightly sideways — far squarer than boxing. Both hips should be visible to the opponent.
Put about 60–70 percent of your weight on the rear leg. Lift the lead heel slightly so the lead foot is light on the ball.
Keep both knees soft, not locked and not sitting low.
Raise both gloves to brow height, a fist's width in front of the face, with the elbows down and in, covering the ribs.
Tuck the chin and look at the opponent's chest, so you see hands and feet together.
keyPoints: Weight back is the whole point: the lead leg must be able to lift instantly to check a low kick or throw a teep.
Stand tall. A low, crouched boxing stance makes your legs a target and slows your kicks.
Gloves higher than in boxing, at the brow — elbows and head kicks are coming.
Elbows stay close enough to the body that a body kick lands on the arm, not the ribs.
Many Thai fighters keep a gentle rhythm, rocking forward and back on the rear leg; stay relaxed rather than rigid.

moves.title: Shin Block (Check)
moves.summary: Lift the knee and turn the shin out so a roundhouse lands shin-on-shin, with the elbow and knee closing the gap above it.
steps: From the stance, with the weight already on the rear leg, lift the lead knee up and slightly out toward the incoming kick.
Turn the shin out so it faces the kick, toes pointed slightly out and the foot tense.
Bring the lead elbow down to the knee, so arm and leg make one wall from head to shin.
Keep the rear glove high on the brow and the standing knee slightly bent.
Absorb the kick, then put the foot straight back down in the stance, ready to counter.
keyPoints: Lift the knee high: check with the upper shin, near the knee, which is the strongest part.
The weight must already be on the rear leg; a check that needs a weight shift is late.
Close the gap between elbow and knee for a body kick.
Check the kick, do not reach for it with the leg.
Counter straight away: the kicker is on one leg and turned away from you.

moves.title: Straight Knee
moves.summary: The rear knee driven straight up and forward into the body, powered by the hips, with the hands pulling the target down onto it.
steps: From the stance, reach forward with both hands toward the opponent's head or shoulders.
Rise onto the ball of the lead foot.
Drive the rear knee straight up the centre line, toes pointed down, heel tucked to the buttock.
Push the hips forward and lean the shoulders back, pulling down with the hands at the same moment.
Lower the foot back behind you to the stance.
keyPoints: The hips drive the knee: push the belt buckle forward into the target.
Point the toes down; it tightens the leg and keeps the point of the knee leading.
Pull with the hands as the knee rises, so the two forces meet.
Stand tall on the ball of the standing foot.
Against an opponent walking in, the knee meets them; you do not need to chase.

moves.title: Teep: Lead and Rear
moves.summary: The push kick: knee up, then the hips push the ball of the foot straight through the opponent's belly. Muay Thai's jab with the legs.
steps: From the stance, lift the knee of the kicking leg straight up toward your chest, toes pulled back.
Push the hips forward and extend the leg straight out, striking with the ball of the foot (or the whole sole for a push).
Lean the shoulders back just enough to counterbalance; stay on the ball of the standing foot.
Pull the knee straight back to the chest along the same line.
Put the foot back down in your stance, or step it forward if you want to follow up.
keyPoints: Knee first, then the foot. Lifting the knee is what keeps the teep straight and hard to catch.
The power is the hip thrust, not the leg alone.
Aim at the belly or the hip of the lead leg as the opponent steps forward: it stops them.
Retract fast; a teep left out is easy to catch.
Keep the hands up; the lead-side hand may drop slightly for balance, the other stays on the brow.

moves.title: Uppercut
moves.summary: A rising punch up the centre line, driven by the legs, that splits a high Thai guard and catches an opponent leaning in.
steps: From the stance, bend both knees slightly and drop the rear shoulder a little, keeping the glove at the chin.
Drive up with the legs and turn the rear hip forward.
Let the rear fist rise on the centre line, palm facing you, elbow bent.
Land under the chin or into the body, then return the glove straight to the brow.
The lead glove stays high throughout.
keyPoints: The power comes from the legs straightening, not from the arm.
Keep the dip small. A big dip is a telegraph and drops your head into knee range.
Keep the elbow bent; a straight-arm uppercut is a weak scooping push.
It is a close-range punch: use it when the opponent is leaning in or reaching to clinch.

moves.title: Uppercut Elbow (Sok Ngat)
moves.summary: The elbow driven straight up the centre line into the chin, after a short dip of the knees, like an uppercut with the arm folded.
steps: From the guard at close range, dip by bending the knees; the elbow drops low and tucks in.
Drive up with the legs and bring the elbow up the centre line, fist passing your ear.
Strike the chin with the point of the elbow.
Bring the arm back down to cover.
Return to the guard.
keyPoints: The legs drive it up, not the shoulder.
Up the centre line, between the opponent's gloves.
The dip is short. A deep dip is slow and easy to read.
Keep the other glove on your face.
In the clinch, it is the answer to an opponent who puts their head down.

moves.title: Attention Stance
moves.summary: The attention stance is the formal standing position used at the start and end of class, before bowing, and between commands — heels together, toes out at 45°.
steps: Stand upright with heels touching or nearly touching.
Turn the toes out equally so that the feet form a V-shape at approximately 45° total (22.5° each side from the centerline).
Lock the knees straight — legs are fully extended, not bent.
Let the arms hang naturally at the sides, hands loosely closed into light fists or open, fingers together.
Keep the chin level, eyes forward, shoulders back and relaxed, spine straight.
keyPoints: Heels are together (or touching) — this is the key distinction from ready stance.
The V-angle of the feet is modest — not a wide splay. Roughly 45° total.
The body is upright but relaxed, not rigidly tensed.
Arms hang at the sides — do not clasp hands in front or behind the body.
This stance is held still; fidgeting or looking around is considered disrespectful.

moves.title: Back Stance
moves.summary: The back stance loads 70% of the weight onto the rear foot, keeping the front leg light for quick kicks — paired with knife-hand blocks in poomsae.
steps: Step forward with one foot so the feet are roughly one-and-a-half shoulder-widths apart (shorter than front stance, similar depth to walking stance).
Rotate the rear foot 90° outward so it points perpendicular to the direction of facing.
Bend the rear knee deeply over the rear foot — the rear knee should be above the toes of the rear foot.
Place the front foot pointing directly forward, with only a slight bend in the front knee — the front leg is mostly extended.
Distribute weight: 70% on the rear foot, 30% on the front foot.
Keep the hips at roughly 90° to the direction of facing — the body turns more to the side than in front stance.
keyPoints: The 70/30 weight distribution is fundamental — without it, the front leg cannot kick quickly.
The rear knee is the loaded, bent knee; the front knee is nearly straight and light.
The rear foot is at 90° to the direction of the front foot — perpendicular, not at 45°.
The front foot remains in contact with the floor but bears minimal weight.
The hips naturally turn about 90° from forward-facing when the rear foot is set correctly.

moves.title: Fighting Stance
moves.summary: The fighting stance is the dynamic guard position used in sparring — weight distributed 50/50, lead foot forward, hands raised to protect the head and body.
steps: Step one foot forward (typically the left for a right-handed practitioner, but lead with whichever foot is natural).
Turn the body roughly 45° toward the opponent — not square-on and not fully sideways.
Place feet shoulder-width apart both laterally and forward-to-back. The stance is shallower than a walking stance.
Bend both knees slightly — the weight is on the balls of the feet, not the heels.
Distribute weight approximately 50/50 between both feet.
Raise both hands into guard: the rear hand protects the jaw and chin, the lead hand is extended slightly in front of the face or chest. Both fists are loosely clenched.
Keep the elbows tucked down to protect the ribs. Shoulders are relaxed, not raised.
keyPoints: The stance is upright and mobile — this is not a deep, rooted stance. You should be able to bounce slightly on the balls of the feet.
The body angle (roughly 45°) reduces your frontal target area, making it harder for an opponent to score on the trunk protector.
The lead (front) hand provides distance control and sets up combinations; the rear hand protects the face.
Keep the chin slightly down and the eyes over the top of the lead fist — never drop the guard to look at the opponent's feet.
In competition sparring, practitioners often stand more upright and side-on than in poomsae stances.

moves.title: Front Kick
moves.summary: The front kick is the most fundamental kick in Taekwondo — a straight, snapping kick driven by the ball of the foot.
steps: Begin in your fighting stance with your non-kicking foot forward and hands raised in guard position.
Shift your weight onto your supporting leg and raise your kicking knee up toward your chest — this is the "chamber" position.
From the chamber, snap the foot forward and extend the leg, striking with the ball of the foot (the padded area just below the toes).
Retract the foot back to the chambered position immediately after contact — do not drop the leg straight down.
Return to fighting stance by placing the kicking foot either forward (stepping through) or back to its starting position.
keyPoints: Keep the toes pulled back to expose the ball of the foot as the striking surface.
The kicking knee should rise as high as possible before extension — the power comes from the snap, not a swing.
Keep your guard up throughout the kick; do not drop your hands.
Stay on the ball of your supporting foot to allow hip rotation.
The kick should be a sharp snap, not a push — retract fully.

moves.title: Front Stance
moves.summary: The front stance is a deep, forward-weighted power stance used in poomsae for delivering strikes and blocks with maximum grounding and body mass behind them.
steps: Step forward so there is approximately two shoulder-widths of distance between the front heel and the rear toes (significantly longer than walking stance).
Bend the front knee deeply until the thigh approaches 45° from vertical — the knee should be directly above the toes of the front foot, not caving inward.
Keep the rear leg fully extended and straight — locked at the knee, no bend.
The front foot points directly forward. The rear foot turns outward at roughly 45°.
Distribute weight approximately 60–70% on the front foot, 30–40% on the rear.
Keep the hips squared forward, spine upright. The torso does not lean forward over the front knee.
keyPoints: The front knee must not cave inward (knee valgus) — it tracks directly over the middle toe of the front foot.
The rear leg is straight and extended — any bend in the rear knee shortens and weakens the stance.
The stance is significantly longer and lower than walking stance. Beginning students often make it too short, turning it into a glorified walking stance.
Hips stay squared forward — do not allow the hips to twist toward the rear foot.
The depth (how far the front knee bends) should allow the thigh to approach 45° without the heel lifting off the floor.

moves.title: High Block
moves.summary: The high block deflects downward strikes aimed at the head by driving the forearm upward and forward above the forehead.
steps: Begin in walking stance or fighting stance with hands in the guard position.
Bring the blocking arm across the body — the fist starts near the opposite hip, palm inward, like a wind-up position.
Simultaneously begin pulling the reaction hand back toward its hip, palm-up.
Drive the blocking arm upward in an arc — the forearm crosses in front of the face as it rises.

Finish with the forearm above and slightly in front of the forehead, the fist at forehead level or higher. The arm is angled roughly 45° — elbow bent, forearm tilted forward, palm facing outward and slightly upward.
Kime (tighten) at the moment of completion. The elbow should not be directly above the head — keep it offset to prevent a strike from driving your own arm into your skull.
keyPoints: The finishing position has the forearm angled forward at about 45°, not horizontal over the head.
The fist should be above the top of the forehead, one to two fist-widths above the head.
The blocking surface is the outside of the forearm (the same side as the little finger).
Keep the reaction hand sharp and simultaneous — it multiplies the speed of the block.
Eyes remain level and visible; do not raise the arm so high it blocks your vision.

moves.title: Knife-Hand Block
moves.summary: The knife-hand block deflects attacks using the outer edge of the open hand, executed from back stance — one hand blocks while the other guards at the solar plexus.
steps: Begin in back stance (Dwitkubi): weight 70% on the rear foot, lead foot pointing forward, rear foot at 90°.
Raise the blocking hand (the lead-side hand) to the opposite ear — palm faces outward, elbow bent, fingertips pointing up.
Place the guard hand extended forward at solar plexus height, palm upward and open.

Execute the block: sweep the lead hand in an arc downward and outward, finishing with the knife edge of the hand at shoulder height on the blocking side, forearm angled slightly downward (about 30° below horizontal). The palm faces away from the body at the finish.
Simultaneously draw the guard hand back to solar plexus level, palm now facing upward — the guard hand does not pull all the way to the hip.
Kime at the point of completion.
keyPoints: The blocking surface is the knife edge of the open hand — the outer edge from the base of the little finger to the heel of the hand. Fingers are held together and slightly bent (not rigidly straight).
The guard hand stays at solar plexus height with the palm open, not pulled to the hip like in fist techniques. This is what makes the technique visually distinctive.
The block finishes at roughly shoulder height on the blocking side — not at face level and not at the hip.
The motion is a sweeping arc, not a straight push outward.
Back stance is required — the weight distribution (70% rear) is part of the technique.

moves.title: Low Block
moves.summary: The low block deflects attacks aimed at the lower body — particularly kicks — by sweeping the forearm downward across the body.
steps: Begin in walking stance (Ap Seogi) or fighting stance with both hands in the starting position near the opposite hip.
Raise the blocking arm across the body with the fist at shoulder height, palm facing inward — this is the wind-up position.
Simultaneously bring the opposite (non-blocking) arm back to hip level, fist palm-up (this is the "reaction hand" or Bandae).
Drive the blocking forearm downward in a sweeping arc, finishing with the forearm angled at roughly 45 degrees below horizontal, fist facing down, positioned in front of the thigh.
Tighten (kime) at the moment of completion — the block should end with tension, not a relaxed drop.
keyPoints: The blocking arm must pass in front of the body, not to the side — deflection happens across the centerline.
Finish with the fist about one fist-width above and in front of the knee, not resting on the thigh.
The reaction hand pulling back to the hip generates equal and opposite force, increasing the speed and power of the block.
Keep the blocking elbow slightly bent at the end position — never lock the elbow out fully.
In poomsae, the block is executed in walking stance simultaneously with a step forward.

moves.title: Middle Block
moves.summary: The middle block sweeps the forearm inward across the body to deflect attacks aimed at the midsection.
steps: Begin in walking stance or fighting stance.
Wind up by raising the blocking arm — the fist starts at ear level on the same side, palm facing inward toward the head, elbow pointing outward.
Drive the forearm inward and slightly downward in an arc across the centerline of the body.
Simultaneously pull the reaction hand sharply to the opposite hip, palm-up.
Finish with the forearm vertical (or slightly angled), the fist at shoulder height on the blocking side, elbow bent at roughly 90°. The palm faces inward (toward the body).
Kime at full extension.
keyPoints: The blocking surface is the inside of the forearm (the thumb side / radial bone).
The fist finishes at the same height as the shoulder — not at face level, not at navel level.
The elbow should be about a fist-width from the body — do not press the elbow into the ribs.
The forearm should be roughly vertical at the end, not horizontal — the angle deflects a punch out to the side.
The winding motion is important: starting from ear height generates the arc that creates deflective power.

moves.title: Ready Stance
moves.summary: The ready stance is the default standing position between techniques — feet shoulder-width apart, fists held in front of the body at belt level.
steps: From attention stance, step one foot out to the side so the feet are approximately shoulder-width apart.
Both feet point directly forward, parallel to each other.
Distribute weight evenly — 50% on each foot. Knees are straight but not locked rigidly.
Bring both fists in front of the body at approximately belt level (just below the navel), knuckles facing downward (palms facing inward).
The elbows are slightly bent and relaxed — arms are not rigidly extended.
Keep the upper body upright, chin level, eyes forward.
keyPoints: The fists are held at belt level in front of the body — not at the hips, not raised to chest height.
Palms face inward (toward each other), knuckles down.
Feet are parallel and shoulder-width apart — unlike attention stance where the heels touch and toes splay.
The stance signals calm readiness — breathing should be relaxed.
In poomsae, the performer returns to ready stance at the end of the form before bowing.

moves.title: Reverse Punch
moves.summary: The reverse punch drives the rear hand forward across the body, generating power from hip rotation — the opposite hand to the lead foot.
steps: Begin in left walking stance (left foot forward). The left fist is extended from a previous technique, the right fist is chambered at the right hip, palm-up.
Without stepping, initiate a sharp rotation of the hips — drive the right hip forward and the left hip back.
As the hip rotates, drive the right fist forward in a straight line toward the target (solar plexus height for a body punch, face height for a face punch).
Rotate the fist 180° during the punch — palm-up at the hip, palm-down at full extension. The rotation happens at the end of the motion, not the beginning.
Simultaneously pull the left fist sharply back to the left hip, palm-up (reaction hand / Bandae).
Kime at the moment of full extension, tightening the forearm, wrist, and shoulder.
keyPoints: The power source is the hip, not the shoulder. If the hips don't rotate, the punch is arm-only and loses most of its force.
The elbow tracks close to the body throughout — it does not flare out sideways.
The wrist rotates at the very end; starting the rotation too early wastes the snap.
The reaction hand (pulling back the left fist) is as important as the punching hand — it creates equal and opposite momentum.
In poomsae, the reverse punch often follows a block in the same stance rather than a step.

moves.title: Roundhouse Kick
moves.summary: The roundhouse kick swings the leg in a horizontal arc, striking with the ball of the foot or instep — the signature technique of Taekwondo sparring.
steps: Begin in fighting stance.
Raise the kicking knee upward and forward — chamber with the knee pointing toward the target (or slightly past it). The higher the knee rises, the higher the kick can reach.
Pivot on the supporting foot, rotating the heel toward the target. This hip rotation is what converts the knee-lift into a horizontal arc.

Swing the lower leg outward in a snapping arc from the knee — the foot travels horizontally and strikes the target with the ball of the foot. The ankle is plantar-flexed (foot pointed, toes back) to expose the ball, or dorsiflexed (foot flexed) to use the instep.
Snap the lower leg back at contact — do not push through the target, snap into it.
Lower the foot to the ground, returning to guard. Do not let it drop; control the return.
keyPoints: The knee chamber determines the height — chamber low for a body kick, chamber at face height for a head kick. Many beginners try to "lift" the kick at the end; the height is set by the chamber, not the extension.
The pivot of the supporting foot is essential. If the heel doesn't turn to face the target, the hip cannot rotate and the kick becomes a forward-swinging leg swing rather than a proper roundhouse.
The snapping retraction at contact multiplies the percussive force and makes the kick harder to catch.
In sparring (with foot protectors), the instep is the more practical striking surface. In poomsae and self-defence, the ball of the foot is preferred.
Eyes remain on the target throughout — do not look at the floor when pivoting.

moves.title: Side Kick
moves.summary: The side kick thrusts the heel and outer edge of the foot directly into the target from the side, generating power through hip extension and chamber.
steps: Begin in fighting stance or walking stance.
Lift the kicking knee up toward the chest — this is the chamber. The knee points directly at the target. The foot is flexed, toes pulled back, heel forward.
Pivot on the supporting foot so the heel of the supporting foot turns toward the target and the hip of the kicking leg opens up to face the target.

Thrust the kicking leg out in a straight line toward the target, driving through with the heel as the primary striking surface. The hip thrusts forward as the leg extends — this hip snap is the main power source.
At full extension, the kicking foot, knee, and hip are aligned in a straight line pointing at the target. The body leans slightly away from the target to counterbalance.
Retract the kick back through the chamber position before returning the foot to the ground.
keyPoints: The striking surface is the heel and the outer blade of the foot (the knife edge) — not the ball of the foot and not the toes.
The foot must be flexed (toes back, heel forward) at the point of contact.
Chamber first — the knee comes up before the kick extends. Kicking without a chamber loses both power and height.
The supporting foot pivots: the heel must turn to face the target so the hip can open and drive into the kick.
The lean-back is not a mistake — it is required for balance and to allow full hip extension.

moves.title: Straight Punch
moves.summary: The straight punch delivers a direct thrust with the same-side hand as the front foot, striking with the index and middle finger knuckles.
steps: Begin in left walking stance (left foot forward) with fists at hip level — left fist palm-up at the left hip, right fist extended forward from a previous technique.
Step forward with the right foot into right walking stance while simultaneously chambering the right fist back to the right hip, palm-up.
As the right foot lands, drive the right fist forward in a straight line toward the target (solar plexus height), rotating the fist so the palm faces downward at full extension.
Simultaneously pull the left fist sharply back to the left hip, palm-up — this is the reaction hand (Bandae).
Lock (kime) at the moment of full extension — the forearm, wrist, and shoulder tighten to maximise transfer of force.
keyPoints: The punch must travel in a perfectly straight line — not an arc or haymaker swing.
The wrist rotates 180° during the punch: palm-up at the hip, palm-down at extension. The rotation happens at the very end of the movement.
The elbow tracks close to the body and scrapes past the ribs rather than winging out to the side.
Kime (focus) is essential — a relaxed arm through the motion, a sharp tighten at impact.
In poomsae, the punch lands precisely as the stepping foot touches the ground.

moves.title: Walking Stance
moves.summary: The walking stance is the primary stance used in poomsae — it mirrors a natural walking step and develops hip alignment and balance.
steps: Stand with feet together (Charyot, attention stance) as your starting position.
Step forward with one foot approximately one shoulder-width ahead, keeping the feet parallel (both pointing forward — unlike a wider lunge).
Distribute your weight evenly — 50% on each foot.
Bend the front knee very slightly — the stance is upright, not deeply bent like a front stance.
Keep the hips squared forward, not rotated to the side.
Hold the upper body upright with the head up, chin level.
keyPoints: The feet should be roughly shoulder-width apart both laterally and forward — narrower than a front stance (Apkubi).
Both feet point directly forward, parallel to each other.
The stance is mobile — you should be able to step forward naturally from it, as the name implies.
Weight stays central; this is a transitional and form stance, not a rooted power stance.
In Taeguek poomsae, each step into walking stance is coordinated with a block — the block should land at the same moment as the foot.

moves.title: Level Change
moves.summary: Dropping the hips by bending the knees, not the waist, so your shoulders reach the opponent's hips with your back straight and your head up.
steps: Start in a good stance, hips at the height you wrestle from.
Bend the knees so the hips drop straight down.
Keep the back at the same angle it had in the stance; do not fold forward at the waist.
Keep the head up and the eyes on the opponent's hips.
Keep the elbows in and the hands in front.
keyPoints: Knees, not waist. The back angle in the level change is the same as in the stance.
The head stays up. The hips go down; the head does not go down first.
It should be quick and give nothing away: no wind-up, no shifting of the feet first.
Change levels at the right distance. Dropping too far away is a level change the opponent can watch.
Level-change with feints too, so the drop is not always a shot.

moves.title: Penetration Step
moves.summary: The long, low step that carries you through the opponent's hips: drive off the rear foot, drop the lead knee to the mat, and keep moving forward.
steps: Start in stance and change levels: hips drop, head and chest stay up.
Take a long, low step with the lead foot, pushing hard off the ball of the rear foot.
Let the lead knee come down to the mat, roughly where the opponent's feet are.
Keep the rear leg driving, the back straight and the head up: you are still moving forward when the knee lands.
In the drill, drive off the lead foot back up into stance and repeat. In a takedown the rear leg steps up instead.
keyPoints: Level change first, then the step. The hips go down before they go forward.
The step is long and low. Your shoulder needs to reach the opponent's hips.
The knee lands softly on the mat. It does not crash down; the rear leg is still pushing.
The back stays straight and the head up the whole time, so you drive into the opponent instead of diving under them.
Keep the elbows in; the hands go behind the knees in the real shot.

moves.title: Stance and Motion
moves.summary: The wrestling stance — feet wide and staggered, knees bent, hips under, head up — and how to move in it without ever crossing your feet.
steps: Feet a little wider than your shoulders, one foot slightly ahead of the other (a staggered stance).
Bend the knees until your hips sit low, roughly at the height you would wrestle from.
Keep the hips under you and the back straight, leaning forward from the hips, not rounding over at the waist.
Head up, eyes on the opponent's hips or chest, elbows in, hands out in front at about knee height.
To move forward, step the lead foot first, short and low, then bring the rear foot the same distance.
To move back, step the rear foot first, then the lead foot follows.
keyPoints: The feet never cross and never come together. Each step is followed by the other foot, so the stance is the same after every step.
Steps are short. Long steps leave you on one leg.
Hips stay at one height while you move: no bobbing up and down.
Weight on the balls of the feet, never on the heels.
Elbows in and hands active; they protect your legs and hand-fight theirs.
